The Shutdown Ends, the Pardons Land, and the Epstein Files Force a Reckoning

A week that closed the longest government shutdown in U.S. history while a sweeping wave of pardons and a forced House vote on Epstein records tested the limits of executive power

```markdown The week of November 8 through 14 closed one of the longest standoffs in the federal government's history and opened another, quieter one over what the public is entitled to know about a dead sex offender's ties to the powerful. By Friday, the shutdown was over, dozens of pardons had been issued to allies and donors, and a rank-and-file effort to force disclosure of Justice Department files on Jeffrey Epstein had survived direct presidential pressure to reach the House floor. Courts intervened repeatedly along the way, with uneven effect.

The weekend began with an unusual act of reversal. On Saturday, the Department of Agriculture ordered states to claw back full SNAP payments already delivered to roughly 42 million low-income Americans, after the Supreme Court paused a lower court's order requiring full funding. Democratic governors in Wisconsin, Oregon, and Massachusetts refused outright, arguing the payments were lawfully made and promising to fight the directive in court. The dispute set the tone for the week: an executive branch trying to use a funding lever against a vulnerable population, and state and federal courts pushing back within days.

That same weekend brought the first and most sweeping wave of a mass clemency campaign. On Sunday, pardon attorney Ed Martin announced that Rudy Giuliani, Mark Meadows, Sidney Powell, Jenna Ellis, John Eastman, and 72 others involved in efforts to overturn the 2020 election had been pardoned — 77 people in all, covering federal charges only, timed to land quietly alongside Senate negotiations to end the shutdown. Georgia's state prosecution of the fake-elector scheme remained untouched, but the federal shield for the operation's architects was now complete. The same weekend, Trump floated a string of uncoordinated policy ideas — 50-year mortgages, a $2,000 tariff dividend Treasury's own secretary seemed unaware of, and a health savings account replacement for ACA subsidies — each announced by social media rather than legislation. Separately, Border Patrol Chief Gregory Bovino claimed agents had come under gunfire in Chicago; police found no such evidence, days after a federal judge had already found he lied about a different violent incident.

By Monday, the shutdown's endgame accelerated. The Senate voted 60–40 to advance a funding bill running through January 30, 2026, restoring federal pay and reversing shutdown layoffs, but without any binding extension of ACA subsidies — only a promise of a future vote. Eight Democrats and independent Angus King had broken with their caucus to get there, over the objections of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and progressive holdouts who said the deal secured nothing on healthcare. Buried in the bill was a provision letting Republican senators subpoenaed by former special counsel Jack Smith sue the Justice Department for damages. The same day, Trump threatened to dock pay and deny severance to air traffic controllers who had taken unpaid leave during the shutdown, even as flight cancellations mounted nationally. The pardon campaign widened further, adding a trucking-emissions offender and a broader shield covering all conduct tied to the fake-elector scheme, issued just before a Georgia deadline to name a new prosecutor in that state's case. Courts intervened on two fronts: the First Circuit rejected the administration's SNAP maneuver and ordered emergency reserves tapped, while a Utah judge threw out a Republican-drawn congressional map in favor of a competitive one — prompting a state legislator to file impeachment articles against her. Trump also warned that the government could not afford to comply with an adverse Supreme Court ruling on his tariff authority, inflating the potential cost to $3 trillion and accusing the justices of bias. ICE enforcement drew fresh scrutiny after agents pepper-sprayed a family with a one-year-old in Cicero, Illinois, and a plainclothes agent drew a firearm on a civilian driver in Santa Ana.

Tuesday brought a formal move against an independent watchdog. The Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion arguing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau could no longer draw Federal Reserve funds, since the Fed has operated at a loss since 2022; OMB Director Russell Vought then suspended most of the bureau's operations, notwithstanding a court order blocking mass firings there. The pardon wave turned toward wealth and proximity: George Santos had his fraud sentence commuted after serving only months, billionaire Joe Lewis was pardoned for insider trading, a pharmacist convicted of health fraud tied to a sitting congresswoman's husband was cleared, and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao received clemency amid a $2 billion deal between Binance and a Trump family crypto venture. ICE's Chicago operation escalated further — agents forcibly dragged a worker from a daycare center, swept up landscaping workers and rideshare drivers at O'Hare, and deployed pepper spray near a neighborhood Halloween parade, while a federal judge separately reprimanded Bovino for lying about throwing a gas canister at protesters. Trump's legal team sent the BBC a $1 billion defamation demand over an edited January 6 documentary, days after the network's director general and head of news had already resigned over the controversy. At Fannie Mae, ethics and investigations staff — including the chief ethics officer — were removed while probing whether FHFA Director Bill Pulte had improperly accessed mortgage records of Democratic officials, including New York Attorney General Letitia James; the acting inspector general who had escalated the matter to prosecutors was also pushed out. And ahead of a swearing-in the White House had delayed for weeks, Trump began personally lobbying Republican Representatives Lauren Boebert and Nancy Mace to withdraw their signatures from a discharge petition on Epstein-related records.

Wednesday was the week's hinge. After a delay of more than fifty days, Speaker Mike Johnson swore in Representative Adelita Grijalva of Arizona, who immediately signed the discharge petition on Epstein files, pushing it past the 218-signature threshold needed to force a floor vote — despite the president's active effort to stop it. The same day, the House passed the Senate's shutdown-ending bill 222–209, closing out the funding fight but leaving the ACA subsidy question unresolved; House Democrats promptly filed their own discharge petition on healthcare. Hours later, House Oversight Democrats released Epstein estate emails in which Epstein told associates that Trump "knew about the girls" and had spent hours with a trafficking victim at his home, followed by a larger release exceeding 20,000 pages. The White House dismissed the material as a partisan "hoax." Courts, meanwhile, intervened again on immigration enforcement: a federal judge found the daycare-worker arrest unlawful and ordered a bond hearing, and another judge ordered the release of more than 600 people detained during the Chicago operation, citing violations of a 2022 consent decree. At Fannie Mae, the purge of ethics personnel widened to roughly a dozen staff.

On Thursday, Trump formally signed the bill ending the 42-day shutdown, restoring government operations and back pay through January 30 while leaving the healthcare dispute for another day. House Republican leadership then tried to pass the Epstein Files Transparency Act by unanimous consent, avoiding a recorded vote — Democrats blocked the maneuver, and Johnson announced a full floor vote would occur the following week, declining separately to commit to any House vote on ACA subsidies. Trump pardoned billionaire Joe Lewis outright, citing his age and health, extending the week's pattern of clemency for the wealthy and connected. The State Department designated four European antifa-linked groups as foreign terrorist organizations for the first time, a move that opens the door to expanded surveillance of perceived supporters, including U.S. citizens. In New York, both major mayoral campaigns were found circulating unlabeled AI-generated content, including racist and Islamophobic deepfakes targeting Zohran Mamdani, in apparent violation of state disclosure law. HUD announced cuts to more than half of Continuum of Care homelessness funding, threatening housing assistance for up to 170,000 people, while seven detained immigrants filed a class-action suit alleging life-threatening medical neglect at a California ICE facility.

The week ended with the Epstein fight fully in the open. Trump directed Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate Bill Clinton, Larry Summers, Reid Hoffman, and others named in the released documents — timed just before the Transparency Act vote, a step that could allow the department to invoke an "ongoing investigation" exception to withhold records. He simultaneously withdrew his endorsement of Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene and attacked Representative Thomas Massie over their support for disclosure. During an Air Force One press gaggle, he told a Bloomberg reporter asking about the files to be "quiet, piggy," and separately rebuked an ABC reporter for questioning Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman about the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi. A joint report from Human Rights Watch and Cristosal detailed systematic torture — beatings and sexual violence — of Venezuelans rendered by the administration to El Salvador's CECOT prison, noting that only 3 percent had been convicted of a violent crime in the United States. In a smaller but notable check on executive influence, Indiana's Senate leadership announced it would not hold a special session to redraw the state's congressional map despite pressure from Trump and Governor Mike Braun. And new reporting alleged that DHS had funneled $143 million in advertising contracts to a firm tied to officials' personal connections without competitive bidding, while a Pulte confidant was accused of disclosing confidential Fannie Mae pricing data to a rival, with internal objectors again pushed aside.

Taken as a whole, the week showed two systems moving in opposite directions at once. Formal government function was restored — the shutdown ended, pay resumed, agencies reopened — but the underlying dispute over health subsidies that caused it was simply deferred, not resolved. At the same time, a widening set of executive actions — mass pardons for allies and donors, an attempt to defund an independent regulator, the removal of internal ethics investigators, and a directed investigation of political opponents timed to a transparency vote — tested how far institutional norms could bend before something broke. Courts intervened repeatedly, on food assistance, on detention practices, on redistricting, and largely held their ground when tested. What did not hold as cleanly was the presumption that a discharge petition, a rare tool by which ordinary members of Congress can override leadership and executive pressure alike, would be blocked before it reached the floor. By week's end it had not been blocked. Whether the vote it forced will produce real disclosure, or another round of legal maneuvering to delay it, remained the open question the country carried into the following week. ```
